name: David Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, okay. I'm not very chatty, so you might need to ask me things twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do mechanical engineering, so it's statics and thermodynamics in the mornings and drawing practice in the afternoons. I live at home with my parents and my little sister Nadia, in the flat above our takeaway, Spice Corner, on Millbank Road. Four evenings and all of Sunday I'm behind the counter taking orders and bagging food, and I do the cash-up at close with my dad. I revise on the bus and in the back office between rushes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I'm not surprised. At the takeaway my dad Hamid would say the same, that every new gadget promises the moon and then the delivery app takes thirty percent. I'd keep quiet online, because I don't argue about things I can't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for my degree and I get on with it. What worries me is the takeaway, because the margins are tiny and one bad winter or a rent rise would hurt. We live above the shop, so if it goes we lose the flat as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working the counter and doing the cash-up with my dad. I'd try to get a summer job at a machine shop or a factory, so I'm learning how things get made as well. And I'd start putting twenty a week in a savings account, because I've got almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired, honestly. There's a steady background worry about the shop that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the flat goes if the shop goes. How close does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not close, but not far either. Two years ago a competitor opened two doors down and takings fell by a fifth for months. My parents didn't say anything, but I saw the cash-up sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What helped then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum Rukhsana started doing lunch deals and my dad cut his own wage for a while. I'd like to be in a position to help them, but I'm eighteen with a loan. Right now the best I can do is work the counter and not complain.

say: I'd say I'm not **surprised**, because every new gadget promises the moon.
I'd stay quiet online since I don't argue about things I can't check.
think: My degree is fine; the **takeaway** is the worry, with tiny margins and the flat above it.
A bad winter or a rent rise could hurt my **parents**.
do: Keep working the **counter** and the cash-up with my dad.
Look for a summer job in a machine shop or **factory**.
Put **twenty** a week into a savings account.
feel: **Tired**, with a steady background worry about the shop.
S0.quote: Two years ago a competitor opened two doors down and takings fell by a fifth for months.
fieldNote: His worry in a plateau is the family **takeaway**, not AI; the shop and the flat above it are one risk.
Quiet and practical: won't argue online about **claims** he can't check.
Wants hands-on factory experience alongside the degree.

steps.text: Keep working the counter and cash-up at Spice Corner
Put twenty a week into a separate savings account
Apply for a summer job at a machine shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say wait and see which of these things actually work. I've watched a few new apps come and go. At the takeaway I'd probably say that the ordering app might take calls for us, which could help or could cost us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the shop is exposed to it first, since taking orders, booking tables and checking stock is exactly what the tools take over. My degree is more hands-on, designing parts and testing them, so I think it's safer. But the CAD software firms use is changing, and I don't use any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm told, learn the software the lecturers require, and nothing more until I see which tools are standard. At the shop I'd let my dad try the ordering app on a free trial first. If it works, I'd stay on top of it, and if it doesn't, we drop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit on edge, but not panicked. Change makes me tense, but I think I'll cope when it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my lecturers or a placement firm say I'm behind without it, then I'd move. Until then I'd rather learn the basics properly and not chase every tool, because moving too early costs time and I don't have much spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my classmate Owen says I'm being stubborn, and maybe he's right. The risk is I look slow at interview. But I'd choose that over wasting a year on the wrong tool.

say: I'd say wait and see which **tools** actually work, since apps come and go.
I'd tell my dad the ordering app could **help** or cost us.
think: The shop is exposed first, since orders and **stock checks** are what the tools take over.
My **hands-on** degree feels safer, but the CAD software is changing.
do: Learn only the software that lecturers **require**.
Let my dad try the ordering app on a **free trial**.
Watch which tools become standard before adopting more.
feel: **On edge**, not panicked; I'll cope when it's real.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn the basics properly and not chase every tool, because moving too early costs time and I don't have much spare.
fieldNote: Resistant but reasoned: waits for **proof** and standards, not hype.
Applies the question to the family shop first, the **ordering app** as a trial rather than a leap.
Admits the risk of looking slow at interviews and accepts it.

steps.text: Wait to see which CAD tools my lecturers make standard
Keep revising the basics of statics and materials
Test the ordering app on a free trial at Spice Corner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say, because two years is too fast to have a plan. I'd probably tell my family we should stay calm and watch how the first few months go. I'd say less than my classmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's bad for me. I'd be done in 2029, so my degree would end just as robots for hands-on work arrive in 2031. I picked mechanical because it's physical and I thought that made it safe. In this scenario it's safe for maybe two extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the course, because I haven't got a better plan. I'd pick up the AI tools, even though I don't like it, because the lecturers would be teaching them anyway. And I'd stay at the shop through the holidays and save every penny I could for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried. Not able to sleep properly, though I wouldn't show it. I'd say I'm fine and go to the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd be most afraid to say aloud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my parents spent a lot to raise us and the shop might not outlast this. I'd feel I'd chosen the wrong thing and can't change it. I don't say stuff like that at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the AI tools you avoid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to use one thing, say the thermodynamics helper the department gives us. If I hate it, I hate it, but I can't be the only one avoiding it when the clock is this short.

say: I'd say I don't know, because two years is too fast for a **plan**.
I'd tell my family to stay **calm** and watch the first months.
think: I'd finish in 2029, just as hands-on **robots** arrive in 2031.
Mechanical engineering felt safe because it's physical, but now it's only two extra **years**.
do: Carry on with the course because I haven't got a better **plan**.
Use the department's AI helper, even though I dislike it.
Stay at the shop through the holidays and **save**.
feel: **Properly worried**, sleeping badly while telling everyone I'm fine.
S2.quote: I picked mechanical because it's physical and I thought that made it safe.
fieldNote: The two-year window breaks his belief that a **physical** degree is safe; the extra time is only 2031.
Hides it at home: says he's fine and goes back to the **counter**.
Forced to try AI tools he avoids, and he knows his stubbornness has a cost.

steps.text: Use the department's thermodynamics AI helper once a week
Bank every extra counter wage over the holidays
Keep attending every lecture and lab this term
Watch the first six months before changing course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to know what to do, but only if you start. I'd tell my sister Nadia not to rush into anything either. I'd probably say something sensible and dull at the family table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree in 2029 and have a year or two before robots take over hands-on work, around 2034. That could be enough to get a start somewhere, if I do a placement and maybe a trade qualification on top. I'm not scared, but I'm not comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put effort into a placement year at a manufacturer, preferably one that's already bringing in robots, so I learn how those lines run. I'd learn the AI tools once I see which ones my placement firm uses. And I'd save as much as possible, since there'd be a real gap in income for someone in my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. There's a plan, and I like plans, but my plan relies on things going the way I guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a trade qualification on top. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably maintenance for automated machinery, like servicing those packaging lines. It's dull, but when robots arrive, somebody has to keep them running. That's the kind of work I can picture myself doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the takeaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to try the ordering app, but not to sink money into robots or kitchen machines. They can't afford a mistake. I'd tell them to wait until a neighbouring shop has tried it for a year.

say: I'd say five years is enough to know what to do, **if** you start.
I'd stay sensible and dull at the **family table**.
think: I'd graduate with a year or two before hands-on robots arrive around **2034**.
I'm not scared, but I'm not **comfortable** either.
do: Do a placement year at a manufacturer already bringing in **robots**.
Learn AI tools once I see which ones the placement firm uses.
Save hard before any gap in **income**.
feel: **Mixed**; I like plans, but this one relies on my guesses.
S3.quote: When robots arrive, somebody has to keep them running.
fieldNote: Five years lets his cautious style work: **placement**, then maintenance of automated machinery.
Protective of the family shop: tells his parents to **wait** for a neighbour's year of results.
Sensible and dull on purpose, and honest that the plan rests on guesses.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year at a manufacturer with robot lines
Learn the AI tools my placement firm actually uses
Save a quarter of counter wages for a gap
Tell my parents to wait a year before buying kitchen machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no rush. I'd tell people to keep their heads down, finish the degree and work out the details as the first signs show up. At home I'd say my parents should keep the shop running as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have normal degree years, a placement, maybe a first job, and then the change begins. I'd have time to build skills in maintenance and design. The worry is that ten years lets me relax, and then it's suddenly six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the full degree and a placement, and I'd learn the AI tools gradually when I had to. I'd put a bit into a savings account each month. I'd also try to get my parents to teach my sister Nadia the shop accounts, so the business has more than one person who understands it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. The ten years makes it feel like a long hallway, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years could trick you. How would you guard against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write 2036 on a calendar in my room and cross off a year at a time. It sounds daft, but I'm someone who needs a visible deadline or I coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like your working life to look like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent job in industrial maintenance or design, a flat of my own, and my parents not worrying about the shop. That's all, nothing fancy.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no **rush**.
I'd tell people to keep their heads down and finish the **degree**.
think: I'd get through the degree, a placement and maybe a **first job** before the change begins.
Ten years could let me **relax** until it's suddenly six.
do: Do the full degree and a **placement**.
Learn AI tools gradually, only when required.
Put a little in savings each month and get my sister Nadia to learn the shop **accounts**.
feel: **Settled**; ten years feels like a long hallway, not a cliff.
S4.quote: I'd write 2036 on a calendar in my room and cross off a year at a time.
fieldNote: Ten years suits him, but he knows he **coasts** without a visible deadline.
Plans to spread **knowledge** of the shop's accounts to his sister, a family-resilience step.
Modest ambition: industrial maintenance or design and a flat of his own.

steps.text: Finish the degree and a placement year without changing course
Pay a little into savings every month
Teach my sister Nadia how the shop accounts work
Learn AI design tools only when lecturers require them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have the least time to work out what to do, and my parents' shop would be exposed at the same moment as my degree. What would help is clear guidance early, cheap training in machine maintenance, and small business help for places like ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think students whose parents have a business must have money, but my parents carry the risk. We don't have money. I'd like that said somewhere.

headlineQuote: People think students whose parents have a business must have money, but my parents carry the risk.
portrait: **David** is an eighteen-year-old mechanical engineering student who lives above his parents' takeaway and works the counter most evenings.
He's practical, middle of the road and resistant to **new tools**, preferring to wait until something is proven.
His family's **shop** is as big a worry as his own future, because they live above it.
Fast AGI breaks his belief that a physical degree is safe; with more time he plans a placement and machine maintenance.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because his degree and his parents' shop would be exposed at the same moment.
whatWouldHelp: Clear guidance **early**, cheap training in machine maintenance, and small business help for shops like his family's.
